newsitem.title: USA: GAO unveils BA/American pact air competition plan.
newsitem.headline: GAO unveils BA/American pact air competition plan.

text.p: The U.S. General Accounting Office proposed a plan Wednesday for Heathrow landing and take-off rights that could form the basis for agreement on British Airways' proposed alliance with American Airlines.
The GAO, Congress's investigative arm, outlined a proposal that would give the six U.S. airlines competing with the alliance 23 daily round-trip rights to London's crowded Heathrow Airport.
American and British Airways Plc announced a year ago they intended to form an alliance to market each other's flights as their own and would seek antitrust immunity to do so.
The U.S. Department of Transportation has a policy of only approving such alliances if there is an "open skies" agreement between the U.S. and the countries involved that allow liberal access.
Critics of the American-BA alliance say the combination will dominate trans-Atlantic routes and lead to higher fares.
GAO said its proposal would increase competition but in testimony prepared for delivery to a Senate aviation subcommittee it noted the considerable obstacles.
While some Heathrow slots could become available in the short term, it would take several years for slots to open up at Heathrow which is generally operating at maximum capacity.

"As a practical matter, therefore, in addition to acquiring some slots under current procedures, the six U.S. airlines will likely need to have slots transferred to them from American Airlines and British Airways," GAO said.

GAO said the two partners have said they expect to be paid fair market value for those slots, yet European Union officials interpret EU regulations as prohibiting the buying and selling of slots and are in dispute with Britain on this.

"As a result of the challenges inherent in addressing the barriers to entry at Heathrow, significant intergovernmental agreement will be needed well beyond the scope of a traditional open skies accord," said GAO director of transportation issues, John Anderson.
European competition commission Karel Van Miert said on Tuesday that the European Commission was unlikely to rule on the alliance before the end of August.
Robert Crandall, chairman of American's parent, AMR Corp, said Wednedsay that he did not know what the attitude of the newly elected Labour Party government in Britain would be.

"The new ministers are taking a look at it and we hope that the Labor government would agree with us that this is a good deal for consumers and for both countries and for both airlines and will support us going forward," he told Cable News Network.
GAO said the potential alliance of American and BA, the two largest carriers in the U.S.-Britain market, "raises significant competition issues."
In 1996 the two airlines accounted for 60 percent of the scheduled passenger traffic between the U.S. and Britain.

"In addition, they currently provide over 70 percent -- and in some cases all -- of the service between Heathrow and several key U.S. gateways, including New York, Chicago, Boston and Miami," GAO said.

Crandall and BA chairman Robert Ayling along with top officials from Virgin Atlantic Airways Ltd and US Airways Group Inc were also due to testify before the Senate Commerce Committee aviation subcommittee later Wednesday.
